title: Directed evolution of laccase from Thermus thermophilus HB27 reveals a variant with enhanced high temperature catalytic activity and electrochemical properties
abstract: Laccases belong to the multicopper oxidase family (MCO). Compared with fungal laccases, bacterial laccases have high stability and activity under extreme pH and temperature conditions. Because of these characteristics, bacterial laccases have become highly impactful in industrial processes. In the present work, we engineered the Thermus thermophilus HB27 laccase (Tth-Lac) by directed evolution. The library had a size of 1.2 x105 colonies, and we screened mutants by malachite green decolorization on solid medium. The results showed that Q36H mutant exhibited higher catalytic activity than Tth-laccase (WT) at 90 degrees Celsius. Both enzymes showed similar pH profiles, but the activity at 90 degrees Celsius of Q36H mutant was X-fold higher than that of the wild-type enzyme. In contrast, the kinetic constants were similar for both enzymes. In the voltammetric responses, at 61.5 degrees Celsius, the Q36H mutant showed increased current, and the T1 copper potential shifted by 100 mV relative to the tth-Lac. These results suggest that the Q36H mutation has high potential for industrial applications because replacing a glutamine (Q) with a histidine (H) at position 36 enhances the enzyme's structural stability, allowing it to function efficiently under extreme temperature conditions.

title: Strategies for Overcoming the Purification Challenges of Meis1 and HoxA9 and Their Functional Characterization
abstract: Transcription factors are critical regulators of homeostasis, and disruption of their function is a common underlying mechanism in cancer. The homeobox Myeloid ecotropic integration site-1 (Meis1) and its binding partner Homeobox A9 (HoxA9) are among the most highly dysregulated transcription factors in cancer, particularly in Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). Upregulation of HoxA9 is observed in more than 50% of AML cases and is a predictor of poor prognosis. Meis1 forms a cooperative DNA complex with HoxA9 and is required for HoxA9-mediated leukemogenesis.

title: Pre-neuronal origins of monoamine and acetylcholine synthesis and transport
abstract: Neuronal architecture is highly modular and individual components can be found in non-neuronal cell types or even neuronless animals, suggesting some functions predate neurons. However, the evolutionary origins of neurotransmitter synthesis, transport and synaptic vesicle biogenesis outside animals remain obscure. To our knowledge, no previous work has systematically addressed the function of neuronal protein homologs outside animals. Our phylogenetic analysis indicates that orthologs of synaptic vesicle (SV) neurotransmitter transporters (SLC18) and synthesis enzymes are widespread in fungi, which, together with animals and sister taxa, form the clade Opisthokonta. Comparing them with their synaptic counterparts can shed light on the emergence of key functions at the animal-fungi split. Here, we combine extensive phylogenetic profiling and statistical analysis with the generation of functional data for these protein families in fungi. We show that monoamine synthesis, orthologous to that of neurons, is present in fungi and places its origin in the opisthokont common ancestor. We also annotate the orthologs of SLC18 transporters showing that they retain an exporter profile and reside predominantly in the endolysosomal system. Building on this observation, we couple deep-learning localization predictions and GO enrichment analysis to show that the phylogenetic context of SVs is lysosomal throughout the Opisthokonta tree, with implications for their phylogenetic origin. In addition, we monitor fungal gene expression in the presence of monoamines showing that they modulate secondary metabolism, hinting at their physiological significance in a neuronless clade. We propose that the machinery associated with neurotransmission originated before animals.

title: Assembly and activation of the AAA+ motor of the multi-subunit cobaltochelatase
abstract: Cobalamin is a complex yet essential cobalt-containing cofactor synthesized exclusively by prokaryotes and archaea. Aerobic cobalamin biosynthesis requires the CobNST multi-subunit class I cobaltochelatase for cobalt incorporation. Cobalt chelation is dependent on the energy transfer from the CobST AAA+/VWA motor unit to the substrate-binding catalytic unit (CobN). However, the mechanism for assembly and function of CobNST cobaltochelatase remains poorly understood. Here, we used cryo-EM to solve the structures of the AAA+ motor CobS, in the absence and presence of ATP and its VWA-partner protein CobT. Our data reveal that the AAA+ CobS assembles into various conformations, including hexameric planar rings and different spiral left-handed assemblies: hexamers, double rings and filaments. In the absence of nucleotide, the CobT N-terminal domain interacts with CobS left-handed oligomers, remaining in a half-assembled, nonfunctional motor unit. In the CobST complex, ATP induces conformational rearrangement of CobS from left-handed helical oligomers to a right-handed closed hexamer. The simultaneous repositioning of the CobT VWA domain to the AAA+ central pore shifts the motor unit to a functional state, ready-to-drive CobN-catalyzed chelation reaction. These findings define the mechanism for assembly and activation of the class I cobaltochelatase CobST motor.

title: Nanoscale identification of organic pigments in biogenic calcite by atom probe tomography
abstract: Spatially-resolved mass spectrometry could contribute to the understanding of biological processes. Atom probe tomography (APT) is a technique which could, in principle, fill an analytical gap for nanoscale mass spectrometry. Yet, because of a limited understanding of the process of fragmentation of biomolecules, biological or biochemical interpretation of the obtained data has so far not been successful. Here, we report on analyses of synthetic and biogenic pigmented calcite minerals. The purple coloration of Sphaerechinus granularis sea urchin spines is due to the occlusion of polyhydroxylated naphthoquinone (PHNQ) molecules, mainly spinochrome A, within the calcite phase. Peaks relating to these pigments as well as to other intra-crystalline macromolecules were identified by APT analysis of the purple spine region with comparison to measurements of synthetic calcite single crystals, calcite crystals doped with PHNQ, and the uncoloured (white) region of sea urchin spines. To facilitate the molecular identification of peaks appearing solely in purple-coloured spines, which are possible fragments from PHNQ, we introduce novel APT data filtering techniques based on spatial and temporal correlations in the detection of ions of targeted mass-to-charge state ratios. This allows us to discuss the fragmentation of organic molecules under field conditions and improve the identification of peaks in the mass spectrum, while also determining nanoscale spatial distribution of fragments related to specifically targeted biomolecules in 3D and elucidate the relationship these organic pigment molecules have to the calcite lattice and inorganic elements such as magnesium. The study aims to improve identification of complex molecular structures by APT, including organic molecules, with the potential ability to provide structural information at a near-atomic scale for a range of materials.

title: A Tandem Fluorescent Rh1::eGFP mCherry Reporter Reveals Rhodopsin 1 Trafficking and Turnover In Vivo in Drosophila Photoreceptors
abstract: Rhodopsin 1 (Rh1), the major visual pigment of Drosophila photoreceptors, requires a vitamin A-derived chromophore for proper folding, maturation and transport to the rhabdomere. While the endocytic trafficking of mature, light-activated Rh1 to endolysosomal compartments is well characterized, the fate of immature Rh1 during defective ER maturation remains unclear. Here, we developed a Rh1::eGFP-mCherry tandem reporter to monitor Rh1 localization and compartment acidification in vivo. Exploiting the acid stability of mCherry, this reporter enables visualization of Rh1 after delivery to acidic environments and complements conventional antibody-based approaches. Under physiological conditions, pH-dependent quenching of eGFP fluorescence distinguished rhabdomeric Rh1 from Rh1 in acidic endolysosomal compartments. In vitamin A-deficient flies, immature apo-Rh1 accumulated within Calnexin-positive ER membranes, where we identified discrete acidified subdomains characterized by loss of eGFP fluorescence while mCherry fluorescence persisted. These structures remained continuous with the ER but were distinct from conventional endolysosomal compartments, revealing previously unrecognized acidified ER domains associated with immature Rh1. Together, our findings identify acidified ER subdomains as a previously unrecognized stage in Rh1 quality control and establish Rh1::eGFP-mCherry as a robust in vivo reporter for investigating rhodopsin trafficking, maturation and turnover under physiological and disease-relevant conditions.

title: Molecular weaving goes multilevel
abstract: Integrating distinct weaving topologies within a single molecular network creates coupled deformation modes and adaptive adsorption behaviour, pointing to a shift from constructing molecular topologies to exploiting them for functions.

title: Memory Lane: Come to the chemistry show
abstract: Our contributor recalls flamboyant scientific demonstrations to get students excited about chemistry and what inspires audiences today

title: First-Principles Calculations of the Electron-Hole-Pair Creation Energy in Semiconductors and Dielectrics
abstract: We present first-principles calculations of the electron-hole-pair creation energy in semiconductors and dielectrics, focusing in particular on AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2. We have employed density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the band structure, density-functional perturbation theory to obtain the phonon dispersion, and time-dependent DFT (TDDFT) to calculate the electron energy loss function (via the dielectric function). We performed full-band Monte Carlo simulations of electron thermalization for energies up to ~100 eV and calculated the average energy required to excite an electron-hole pair. We calculated pair-creation energies of approximately 12.2, 6.5, 7.3, 3.10, and 16.7 eV/pair for AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2, respectively. These values are in good agreement with measured data, with the largest discrepancy being that of Si (about 14.9% lower than the accepted experimental value of ~3.6 eV/pair). To improve the agreement for Si, we used the GW approach and the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) to calculate the quasiparticle shifts of the electronic band structure and the dielectric function, respectively. Finally, using the GW/BSE data, we calculated a creation energy of ~3.50 eV/pair. We find that the marked improvement in the accuracy of the calculated creation energy, when using the GW/BSE approach, is primarily attributable to the slight decrease in the magnitude of the electron energy-loss function when using the GW/BSE approach for energies below ~10-15 eV. Overall, it is clear that the competition between phonon emission and ionization near the intersection of the phonon scattering and ionization rates is largely responsible for determining the value of the creation energy, with the other major factor being the location and shape of the plasmon peak in the energy-loss function.

title: First-fracture kinetics in periodic chains: from free-energy landscapes and dynamical recrossing to absolute rates
abstract: The nearly collinear configuration of highly stretched polymer chains before fracture motivates one-dimensional models. At fixed extension, stretching one bond redistributes length among the others, coupling rupture to the whole chain. In this work, I develop a framework for fracture-healing rates in periodic Morse chains, combining deterministic theories, equilibrium simulations and a quasi-deterministic approach using equilibrium fluxes and barrier-top trajectories. Constrained-partition calculations closely reproduce simulated populations and intact-state tensions. An intact-reservoir potential of mean force (PMF) supplies the first-fracture surface probability, while recrossing corrects the attempt flux without a rate-fitted prefactor. Independent rate tests identify an operational chain-length boundary for accurate two-state kinetics; failed-return durations decrease relative to population relaxation as chains grow. Kramers-Grote-Hynes (KGH), nonlinear reactive-flux and equilibrium rates show excellent agreement in this regime. KGH predicts rates away from coexistence and a chain-dependent local activation length dominated by the barrier response. Rates decrease approximately exponentially before declining more gently for longer chains: barrier growth dominates, additional fracture sites partly compensate, and transmission varies more weakly. Beyond coexistence, long chains can fracture practically irreversibly because healing becomes too rare to observe. Projected committor crossings, where the configuration-averaged probability of reaching the fractured core first is one half, lie near site-PMF maxima, although configurations at equal bond length retain different fracture probabilities. Multiple fractures remain negligible near coexistence through at least $N=50$. The framework could supply state-dependent rates to mesoscopic fracture models of polymer networks.

title: KNN Implementation Details Can Dramatically Change Performance: An Example from Cover Trees
abstract: Nearest neighbor search algorithms are widely used and have a long history, but we find that key implementation details are seldom reviewed in articles about them. These details can materially impact performance, and thus change the conclusions one makes about a given algorithm's superiority. In this article, we highlight these impacts by reviewing the Cover Tree as an example, producing RustKNN, a unified Rust implementation of three construction variants of the Cover Tree with three query modes. Our analysis reveals: (1) the optimal query strategy depends on $k$ and on the dataset (single-tree search is fastest at $k{=}1$ on three of our four largest datasets, while dual-tree search is fastest at $k{\ge}5$ on the three largest), and choosing the wrong query mode can cost up to a $7.5\times$ factor in runtime; (2) the cover tree base parameter, set to 2 in theory and 1.3 in practice, is not a safe default for dual-tree search: 1.3 is optimal on only one of seven datasets, and on covtype it is $1.6\times$ slower than the optimum; (3) among five micro-optimizations, only early-exit distance computation has a consistent effect, and that effect grows with dimension (none at $d{=}32$, $1.31\times$ at $d{=}54$, and $1.49\times$ at $d{=}784$); and (4) all-nearest-neighbor and held-out benchmarks yield different implementation rankings. All main timing tables report medians over 20 independent allocations with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. RustKNN is open source at https://github.com/CrowdStrike/RustKNN.

title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.

title: High-Efficiency Field-Free Superconducting Diodes in Mo$_2$N/FePt Bilayers
abstract: Near-ideal, field-free superconducting diode behavior is demonstrated in room-temperature-grown Mo$_2$N/FePt bilayers. The response is consistent with remanent FePt stripe domains producing polarity-dependent thresholds for flux entry and vortex motion. Micromagnetic simulations reveal a periodic stray-field modulation across the stripes and asymmetric field enhancement near their ends at the bridge edges. One current polarity remains nearly dissipationless up to a sizable fraction of the estimated depairing current, whereas the opposite polarity develops dissipation at much lower current, yielding diode efficiencies up to approximately 85% in the thinner bilayer. The nonreciprocity can be continuously tuned by the in-plane magnetic preparation angle and reversibly switched by reverse-field excursions through the hysteretic reversal of the FePt layer. These results support edge-controlled flux entry and vortex motion as a route to high-efficiency superconducting diodes.

title: PRAISE: A Reproducible Workflow for Non-Programmer Scientists to Implement Published AI Models
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models are increasingly developed, published and used across scientific fields. Researchers, students and industry professionals who want to apply these models to their own research questions often lack the programming and data science expertise to do so. Existing guidelines cover single steps, but not the route from a published model to working predictions on one's own data. Here we present the hands-on workflow PRAISE, a Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education, that helps non-programmers implement published AI models step by step. Because implementations rarely work the first time, PRAISE anticipates common failures and provides a fallback route for each. As a proof of principle, three BSc chemistry students and their tutor applied PRAISE without prior programming or data science knowledge. They reproduced, validated and extended a state-of-the-art model that predicts enzyme-substrate interactions. This shows that with PRAISE, implementing an AI model from the literature becomes a learnable skill, one that turns non-programmer scientists from users into evaluators and improvers of AI models.

title: A physics-coupled graph neural operator for mid-plane six-component stress tensor field prediction in concrete penetration
abstract: The penetration-resistant design of concrete structures requires the spatiotemporal evolution of the stress field within the target, whereas in design only the strength grade, the geometry and the projectile parameters are known, and the aggregate arrangement is not. Empirical formulae and scalar-output surrogates serve design screening, and mesoscale finite element models resolve the aggregate-scale response, but one solution cannot cover random aggregate samples at scale, and no framework links mesoscale heterogeneity to field-level prediction. A physics-coupled graph neural operator (PC-GNO) is proposed, which learns in function space the evolution of the mid-plane six-component stress tensor field. The training data are generated by full-scale, aggregate-resolved finite element models and comprise 359 cases at the impact velocities of 100, 135 and 165 m/s, corresponding to compressive strengths of 14, 23 and 48 MPa; the data source is verified by laboratory measurements. The coupling strength of message passing is constructed from the impedance contrast across the material interface, and the update is constrained by spectral normalization. Under the single-step primary setting, the mean accuracy of the three levels is 80.16% (91.45%, 77.80% and 71.22%), i.e. 27.81, 42.46 and 34.16 percentage points above the preceding-frame field of the same window; with 20 664 parameters it exceeds the 87.9% of the best Fourier neural operator configuration (about 812 times as many parameters) and the 71.0% of the closed-form linear regression. The output is the complete six-component tensor field rather than a fixed engineering quantity, so that strength criteria and energy indicators follow from one set of weights. For field-level response prediction in concrete penetration, this result provides a data-driven route, with conditions of applicability defined by the training and the evaluation.

title: Intrinsic Geometry Matching: learning observation-equivariant process geometry
abstract: Real data are often arbitrary, indirect observations of an unknown underlying process, and those observations can distort its geometry. Existing geometric methods equip data with the induced geometry of the ambient space, but this entangles the true geometry of the process with the distortion of the observation. To address this, we introduce Intrinsic Geometry Matching (IGM): a scalable approach to learn the intrinsic geometry of the underlying process. Specifically, we learn the carré du champ operator of the process, allowing us to recover its diffusion geometry. Our method uses the fact that data often come with natural perturbations, like steps in a time series, to recover the intrinsic carré du champ while transforming naturally with changes in observation: it is observation-equivariant. Furthermore, since this equivariance relates the geometry of different spaces, we can train a model using additional sources of data, even when that data lies in another space. We evaluate IGM on molecular dynamics, image, and video data and find better performance and scaling than existing neural and graph-based geometric tools.

title: Impact of ligand bulk on conformational rearrangement in supported organometallic complexes
abstract: Measuring the dynamics of surface organometallic species, let alone connecting these to catalysis, is highly challenging. We have applied surface-sensitive proton fast-magic-angle spinning double-quantum sideband NMR methods to probe the dynamics of supported metallocene complexes as a function of ligand size, metal identity, and confinement. It was found that dynamics of these species, which resemble olefin polymerization catalysts, are very sensitive to ligand size and that the complex's orientation is frozen once the bonded alkyl chain reaches a length greater than five carbons.

title: Pre-catalytic activation pathway of the Smc5/6 complex
abstract: The Smc5/6 complex (Smc5/6) preserves genome stability through ATP-dependent DNA organization, but the structural details that prime the complex for productive DNA engagement remain unknown. Here, we combine cryo-electron microscopy and conformational heterogeneity analysis to define the pre-catalytic activation pathway of Smc5/6. We show that in the absence of ATP and DNA, Smc5/6 exists as a heterogeneous conformational ensemble composed predominantly of two conformations termed Bridge and Cross. In the presence of DNA alone, Smc5/6 adopts a Juxtaposed conformation that brings the ATPase heads into proximity, aligning them for nucleotide engagement. With both ATP and DNA associated, Smc5/6 establishes an Engaged architecture, within which DNA stabilizes its head-associated binding cavity through local remodeling of the complex. Conformational heterogeneity analyses suggest a continuous structural transition between the Cross and Juxtaposed states, while anisotropic network modeling identifies the Bridge-Cross-Juxtaposed-Engaged sequence as the mechanically favored pathway connecting the four experimentally observed conformations. Together, these findings support a pre-catalytic conformational pathway for Smc5/6 activation and provide a structural framework for understanding how conformational heterogeneity gives rise to an activation-competent motor state.

title: Multivalent ubiquitin recognition regulates multiple stages of Tau self-assembly
abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) has emerged as an important intermediate in the pathological self-assembly of Tau, yet the molecular mechanisms that regulate this process remain incompletely understood. Although ubiquitin is a prominent component of pathological inclusions in tauopathies and other neurodegenerative diseases, its presence has largely been linked to targeting aberrant proteins for proteasomal or autophagic clearance. Here, we identify Tau as a ubiquitin-binding protein and demonstrate that multivalent, non-covalent ubiquitin recognition regulates multiple stages of Tau self-assembly. Biochemical, biophysical, structural, and computational analyses identified four ubiquitin-binding elements within the Tau microtubule-binding repeat region that engage the canonical hydrophobic patch of ubiquitin, providing a structural basis for multivalent recognition of mono- and poly-ubiquitin species. Functionally, mono- and poly-ubiquitin suppress Tau condensate formation while enhancing the liquid-like properties of condensates that persist. In contrast, mono-ubiquitin selectively enhances aggregation of the disease-linked Tau-P301L variant under conditions without detectable LLPS, demonstrating that ubiquitin exerts distinct effects depending on the molecular context and stage of Tau self-assembly. Together, these findings establish non-covalent ubiquitin recognition as a previously unrecognized mechanism regulating Tau phase behavior and aggregation. More broadly, they expand the role of ubiquitin beyond protein quality control, with ubiquitin architecture providing an additional layer of regulation over Tau condensate formation, dynamics, maturation, and aggregation.

title: Modular Cell-Free Extract Mixing Enables Soluble, Active Biomanufacturing of Difficult-to-Express and Aggregation-Prone Proteins
abstract: Cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) is a powerful platform for rapid protein prototyping and biomanufacturing, but expression of complex proteins remains limited by labor-intensive extract preparation as well as the inability of conventional Escherichia coli extracts to efficiently support disulfide bond formation and prevent protein aggregation. We previously developed a Cell-Free Autoinduction (CFAI) workflow that simplifies extract preparation, however, CFAI-derived extracts retain the folding limitations of standard E. coli systems for producing traditionally difficult proteins. Here, we address these challenges by utilizing extracts enriched with molecular chaperones or Erv1p-based oxidative folding catalysts and combining them through a modular extract mixing strategy to enable independent tuning of the cell-free folding environment. This workflow supplies folding factors through enriched extracts, avoiding recurring purchases of purified supplements and enabling a modeled reagent-cost advantage. To evaluate real-world applications and utility of lysate mixing for protein production, we demonstrate a 10-fold increase in solubility of the aggregation-prone bacterial toxin Colicin M, achieving >95% soluble protein while retaining antimicrobial activity. We further used a Design of Experiments (DoE) framework to optimize combinations of chaperone-enriched and Erv1p-based oxidative folding extracts containing either protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) or DsbC. The optimized compositions produced >95% soluble truncated human tissue plasminogen activator (vtPA), comprising the kringle 2 and protease domains, while preserving enzymatic activity. Together, these results demonstrate that CFAI-derived modular extract mixing provides a tunable, high-throughput strategy with low modeled materials costs for tailoring cell-free biochemical environments for difficult-to-express proteins, expanding CFPS utility for protein engineering and biomanufacturing.

title: Inter-unit variability and rapid depletion of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate in stored red blood cells: implications for transfusion practice in neurocritical care
abstract: Red blood cell (RBC) transfusion aims to restore tissue oxygen delivery, yet a stored unit's capacity to unload oxygen depends on 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), the principal allosteric modulator of hemoglobin-oxygen affinity. Randomized trials comparing fresher with older units have been consistently null, and all have used storage duration as the exposure variable. We asked whether storage age reflects the metabolic state of individual units. Twenty-four leukodepleted packed RBC units were sampled serially from day 3 to day 42 of standard cold storage. 2,3-DPG was quanti-fied by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) with isotopically labelled internal standards, pH was measured in parallel, and trajectories were modelled by linear mixed effects with unit-level random intercepts. At day 3, 2,3-DPG spanned a twenty-fold range across units of identical age (0.8-14.7 mol/g Hb; median 4.8): some were already near-depleted at the earliest sampled timepoint, while others retained near-physiological concentrations. This heterogeneity collapsed rapidly - median val-ues fell to 27% of day-3 levels by day 7 and by more than 90% by day 14 ({beta} = -0.298 mol/g Hb per day, p < 0.001) - and were below the limit of detection in most units af-ter day 17. pH declined monotonically to 6.40 {+/-} 0.04 by day 42 ({beta} = -0.0163 units per day, p < 0.001). Units of identical storage age therefore differ markedly in the metabo-lite that governs oxygen unloading, and virtually all are depleted long before the 42-day expiry, indicating that storage-age dichotomies misclassify the exposure they are intended to represent.

title: Spin Polarization Enhanced Photocatalytic N2 Reduction on Chiral Mesostructured Bi2WO6
abstract: Harnessing the earth-abundant N2 via photocatalysis is a sustainable route to green NH3 synthesis. However, photocatalytic N2 reduction (PNR) remains constrained by the high energy barrier for N2 activation and reduction. In this work, we report that the spin-polarized chiral mesostructured Bi2WO6 (CMB) can facilitate the formation of metastable triplet NOH (3NOH) intermediates, while simultaneously promoting the separation and transport of photogenerated charge carriers, thereby enhancing PNR performance.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Molecular Precursor Chemistry Shapes Early-Stage Reaction Pathways in Nitrogen-Doped Carbon Nanotube Synthesis
abstract: The structural characteristics of carbon nanotubes are usually discussed in terms of processes occurring during nanotube nucleation and subsequent growth from an already formed catalyst nanoparticle. Here, we show that their structural trajectory can begin much earlier, within the first nanoseconds of precursor decomposition and catalyst formation. We combine experiment and reactive molecular dynamics to compare nitrogen-free CNT synthesis with two closely related aromatic nitrogen precursors, pyridine and pyrazine, containing one and two nitrogen atoms per molecule, respectively. Experimentally, both nitrogen-containing precursors promote bamboo-like CNT formation and produce substantially more structurally disordered CNTs than the nitrogen-free reference. Notably, nitrogen incorporation does not scale simply with the amount of nitrogen supplied, demonstrating a strong contribution from precursor chemistry. Reactive molecular dynamics reveals that nitrogen-containing precursors significantly modify local Fe-carbon and Fe-SiO2 interactions during catalyst evolution, while pyridine and pyrazine exhibit distinct decomposition pathways, with pyrazine showing significantly greater decomposition within the simulated timescale. These results demonstrate that precursor chemistry influences the local chemical environment and early catalyst evolution, highlighting its potential role in the initial stages of CNT growth.

title: Exact Gaussian--Hermite closure of the mapping quantum--classical Liouville equation
abstract: In the Meyer--Miller--Stock--Thoss mapping representation, the Liouville operator of the quantum--classical Liouville equation contains an excess coupling term in addition to the Poisson bracket. Neglecting this term yields the Poisson bracket mapping equation (PBME). We expand the mapping dependence of the density in Hermite functions about the Gaussian factor common to all physical mapping densities. In this basis, the excess coupling term acts purely as a raising operator and exactly cancels the raising contribution generated by the back--reaction force. Consequently, the exact dynamics does not generate higher Hermite orders and closes on a finite, sparse system of equations for the coefficient fields. Within the physical sector, these equations reduce to the subsystem quantum--classical Liouville equation. In contrast, the PBME retains the raising contribution of the force, modifying the back reaction within the physical sector while continuously generating higher Hermite orders. For Tully's dual avoided crossing model, direct propagation of the coefficient equations confirms this finite closure and agrees with independent solutions of the subsystem equation. Comparison with converged full quantum dynamics further shows that, across all regimes examined, the PBME is less accurate than the quantum--classical description for populations, coherences, and momentum distributions.

title: Trust-Limited Machine-Learning-Accelerated Nudged Elastic Band Calculations for Small-Polaron Hopping in Rutile TiO2
abstract: Nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations of small-polaron hopping are demanding because nuclear motion is coupled to a self-consistent localized electronic state. Near the charge-transfer region, slow self-consistent-field convergence, localization switching, and competing electronic solutions complicate surrogate-assisted optimization. We develop a Gaussian-process-assisted NEB workflow for this regime and demonstrate electron small-polaron hopping in rutile TiO2 using spin-polarized density functional theory with a Hubbard U correction (DFT+U ) with SIESTA. A joint energy-force Gaussian process (GP) with a Matérn covariance model advances the elastic band, while active-atom root-mean-square and maximum-atom displacement limits constrain surrogate motion relative to evaluated configurations. Reaching these limits triggers first-principles sampling without requiring full surrogate convergence. Three independently DFT-verified 96-atom [001] calculations using 11, 13, and 15 images and different surrogate settings and GP parameterizations yield barriers of 0.1645, 0.1637, and 0.1640 eV, respectively, spanning 0.793 meV. In the 15-image calculation, repeated central-image sampling activates a separately calibrated local GP during surrogate optimization. Final full-band DFT verification gives a maximum projected NEB force of 0.0346 eV/Å. A 324-atom calculation yields a lower barrier of 0.1302 eV, indicating supercell sensitivity and demonstrating feasibility at larger GP observation dimension. The workflow combines controlled surrogate extrapolation, targeted charge-transfer-region interpolation, and independent DFT verification to obtain polaron migration pathways, emphasizing reproducible barriers and full-band force convergence.

title: Potential Molecular Links Between Benzophenone-3 and Breast Cancer: Network Toxicology, Machine Learning, Molecular Modeling, and Gene Expression Validation
abstract: PurposeBenzophenone-3 (BP-3) is a widely used ultraviolet filter with potential carcinogenic concern, but its molecular link with breast cancer remains unclear. This study aimed to identify candidate targets and potential molecular links between BP-3 and breast cancer using toxicological prediction, machine learning, molecular modeling, and gene expression analysis.MethodsThe ADMET and toxicity profiles of BP-3 were evaluated using PubChem, ADMETlab 3.0, ProTox 3.0, and pkCSM. BP-3-related targets were predicted from ChEMBL, STITCH, and SwissTargetPrediction, while breast cancer-related differentially expressed genes were obtained from GEO datasets. Candidate targets were screened by intersection analysis and examined using GO/KEGG enrichment and PPI networks. Core genes were identified using 127 machine learning model combinations and SHAP interpretation. GSVA, GSEA, TIMER2.0, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, MM-GBSA calculations, and qRT-PCR were used for validation.ResultsSeventy BP-3-associated candidate genes related to breast cancer were identified. Among 127 model combinations, Stepglm[both]+SVM showed the best performance, with an average AUC of 0.935, and identified MMP13, ERBB2, and HMGCR as core genes. Functional analyses suggested that these genes were mainly involved in extracellular matrix remodeling, lipid metabolism reprogramming, and energy metabolism regulation. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding poses between BP-3 and the candidate proteins, with docking scores ranging from -5.8 to -8.5 kcal/mol. Molecular dynamics and MM-GBSA analyses indicated stable simulated complexes, with calculated binding free energies below -14.30 kcal/mol. qRT-PCR showed higher expression of MMP13, ERBB2, and HMGCR in the examined breast cancer cell lines than in normal mammary epithelial cells.ConclusionIntegrated computational analyses identified MMP13, ERBB2, and HMGCR as candidate genes potentially linking BP-3 with breast cancer-related molecular features. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations predicted feasible interactions between BP-3 and the corresponding proteins, while qRT-PCR confirmed the differential expression of these genes in breast cancer cell lines. These findings represent computational predictions and correlational evidence rather than proof of direct BP-3 regulation or causation. Direct BP-3 exposure experiments in cellular and animal models are required to establish causal relationships.

title: Molecular Symmetry Decomposition by Graph Automorphism: Fast, Symmetry-Aware RMSD, Structure Alignment, and Canonical Atom Ranks
abstract: The root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) is among the most widely used metrics in computational chemistry. However, computing a chemically meaningful RMSD requires solving a combinatorial “atom mapping” problem: finding the RMSD-minimizing and chemically acceptable correspondence between atoms in two structures. Existing methods force a trade-off. Graph-isomorphism enumeration is exact but can be computationally prohibitive.

title: PolycIMS: Polymers for Automated Cyclic Ion Mobility Spectrometry Calibration
abstract: The development and commercialization of cyclic ion mobility spectrometry (cIMS) instruments has considerably expanded the level of structural details that can be accessed for gaseous ions. Commercial cIMS instruments rely on travelling wave ion mobility spectrometry (TWIMS), a technique that requires calibration of the measured arrival times to enable the determination of collisional cross sections (CCS).

title: ΔNAzyme: A Foundational QM/MM Δ-Machine Learning Potential for Nucleic Acid Enzyme Catalysis
abstract: Nucleic acid enzymes (NAzymes), including ribozymes, DNAzymes, and XNAzymes, are programmable biocatalysts that catalyze diverse chemical reactions and provide unique platforms for investigating catalysis and engineering molecular function. Their central roles in biology and evolution, together with emerging applications in biotechnology, synthetic biology, and medicine, have created an urgent need for predictive computational design frameworks. Although multiscale computational enzymology integrating ab initio quantum mechanics can, in principle, provide predictive insight into these systems, current approaches remain computationally prohibitive for large, complex NAzymes and high-throughput design workflows. Machine learning potentials have the potential to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of multiscale modeling approaches, but QM/MM contexts in which the MM environment is highly polarizing remain challenging. Nucleic acid enzymes present a particularly demanding case: experimentally relevant predictions require an accuracy that semiempirical QM/MM methods alone cannot reliably deliver in their often large, highly charged, metal-dependent active sites. Building on the range-corrected QM/MM Δ-machine learning potential (ΔMLP) framework, we develop ΔNAzyme, a foundational ΔMLP for nucleic acid enzyme reactions. We generate a training set of QM/MM simulations spanning diverse nucleic acid enzyme classes, with energies and forces computed at both the reference (DFTB3) and target (PBE0/6–31G*) levels of theory, yielding a correction on top of DFTB3 that recovers PBE0 quality results. We train models using both the Deep Potential and MACE architectures. The MACE model exhibits enhanced transferability, which we attribute to the equivariant, many-body message-passing framework. Free energy profiles from case-study reactions validate ΔNAzyme against target-level results and show that the model supports efficient fine-tuning to new nucleic acid enzyme systems with minimal additional data.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Machine learning-driven discovery of TGFBR1 inhibitors from Mangifera indica for Atorvastatin-based antidiabetic therapy
abstract: Mangiferin, a C-glucosyl xanthone from Mangifera indica, has known antidiabetic activity, but the specific protein target underlying this activity, and its compatibility with existing antidiabetic drugs such as Atorvastatin, were not defined. In this work, machine learning, network pharmacology, molecular dynamics simulations, and experimental validation identified and validated TGFBR1 as a novel molecular target of Mangiferin and evaluated a Mangiferin-Atorvastatin combination for diabetes therapy.
